title: Integral partial conjugation for an actual longest Weyl representative
statement:
Let $\mathcal R=(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a finite reduced root datum with $\mathbf Q\Phi=M\otimes\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf Z\Phi^\vee=M^\vee$, and $(G,T_{\mathbf Q}=D_{\mathbf Q}(M))$ a split rational realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Fix a base $\Delta$, rational root parameters $p_\alpha$, orderings and integral one-sign groups $E_\pm$ satisfying [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality]. Thus $E_\pm$ are affine spaces over $\mathbf Z$ with polynomial group laws, their generic fibres are the ordered root-product unipotent radicals, and $T_{\mathbf Z}=D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ acts by the root characters [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Set $C=E_-\times_{\mathbf Z}T_{\mathbf Z}\times_{\mathbf Z}E_+$ [def-pc-fibre-product], with coordinate inclusions of $E_-$, $T_{\mathbf Z}$ and $E_+$. Suppose the ordered product $c:C_{\mathbf Q}\to G$ is an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion].

There is an element $n\in N_G(T_{\mathbf Q})(\mathbf Q)$ representing the longest Weyl element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, with these properties. There are opens $W,W'\subset C$, each containing the whole of $E_-$, $T_{\mathbf Z}$ and $E_+$, and morphisms $f:W\to C$, $g:W'\to C$ extending $c^{-1}\operatorname{Ad}(n)c$ and $c^{-1}\operatorname{Ad}(n^{-1})c$ on the generic fibres. Their restrictions give group isomorphisms $E_+\simeq E_-$ and $E_-\simeq E_+$ and inverse torus automorphisms; the restrictions of $g$ are inverse to those of $f$. In particular the torus maps are the monomial maps for $w_0$ and $w_0^{-1}$. On $f^{-1}(W')\subset W$ one has $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}$, and on $g^{-1}(W)\subset W'$ one has $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}$. The coordinate inclusions just mentioned all send their identities to $e=(0,1,0)$, and $f(e)=g(e)=e$. For empty roots take $n=1$, $W=W'=C$ and $f=g=\operatorname{id}$. No multiplication between arbitrary opposite-sign elements of $C$, or group scheme containing $C$, is assumed.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Lemmas 6.3.8--6.3.9, printed pp.220--222: simple-reflection Gauss calculation and induction on a Weyl word. Agent-corrected formulation: use a reduced expression for the actual longest element, not the erroneous product of each simple reflection once in the paragraph preceding Lemma 6.3.9. The inverse map is conjugation by n^{-1}; the displayed inverse compatibility requires that inverse, even where the source repeats n. Read online; WANTED local copy. No Stacks tag states this root-coordinate input.

proof.text: Choose a word for an element carrying $\Phi^+$ onto $-\Phi^+$. Here is the finite argument, avoiding the incorrect source word. The simple-reflection subgroup is finite by [lem-sfb-finite-root-datum-weyl-group]. Choose $w$ in it maximizing $|w\Phi^+\cap(-\Phi^+)|$. A simple reflection $s_a$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{a\}$: its formula changes only the $a$ coefficient in the base, so a positive root other than $a$ still has a positive coefficient elsewhere; reducedness treats roots supported only on $a$. If $w^{-1}a$ is positive, left multiplication by $s_a$ therefore increases the count by one, impossible. Thus every $w^{-1}a$ is negative. Since positive roots are nonnegative combinations of simple roots, $w^{-1}\Phi^+\subset-\Phi^+$, hence equality by cardinality, and $w\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$. Call this element $w_0$ and choose a finite simple-reflection word for it. Minimality of the word is unnecessary.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9, corrected longest-element choice; elementary finite maximization argument in place of the source misprint.

proof.text: For each letter use [lem-sfb-integral-simple-reflection-gauss-chart], writing $h_i=F_{a_i}$ on $V_{a_i}$; order the letters so $w_i=s_{a_i}\cdots s_{a_1}$ and $w_r=w_0$. Set $D_0=C$, $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and recursively $D_i=D_{i-1}\cap H_{i-1}^{-1}(V_{a_i})$, $H_i=h_iH_{i-1}$ on $D_i$. These are open domains and morphisms by composition and inverse images. Inductively $D_i$ contains $T_{\mathbf Z}$ and both $E_\pm$, and $H_i$ maps these last two isomorphically onto $C_{w_i(\pm\Phi^+)}$: at $i=0$ these are exactly $E_\pm$; at the next step the chart's support clause contains the whole intermediate coordinate subscheme in $V_{a_i}$ and identifies its image with the next one. This verifies domain containment as schemes, including every special fibre. The torus remains in every domain because each $h_i$ is the monomial reflection. Set $W=D_r$, $f=H_r$ and $n=n_{a_r}\cdots n_{a_1}$. The chart identifies each $n_a$ with its simple reflection, so $n$ represents $w_0$, and the generic composite is $c^{-1}\operatorname{Ad}(n)c$.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9, printed p.222: explicit domain and coordinate-support induction, using Lemma 6.3.8.

proof.text: Construct the inverse without identifying $n$ and $n^{-1}$. A map for $n_a^{-1}$ is $h_a^3$ on $V_a\cap h_a^{-1}(V_a)\cap(h_a^2)^{-1}(V_a)$, with the powers understood only on their recursive domains. The rank-one chart states $n_a^2=a^\vee(-1)$; because $a^\vee$ is a group homomorphism, $n_a^4=a^\vee(1)=1$. Thus $h_a^3$ is generically conjugation by $n_a^{-1}$. Its three support isomorphisms send $C_P$ successively onto $C_{s_aP},C_P,C_{s_aP}$, so its full domain contains $C_P$ for every such $P$, and also the torus. Apply the recursion of Step 2 to these inverse-letter maps in reverse order. It gives $W'$ containing $E_\pm,T_{\mathbf Z}$ and $g:W'\to C$ generically equal to $c^{-1}\operatorname{Ad}(n^{-1})c$.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9, p.222: reverse inverse word using the fourth-power consequence of the rank-one chart.

proof.text: Since $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$, the final support schemes in Step 2 are exactly $E_\mp$. Thus $f$ and $g$ restrict to isomorphisms of the two one-sign schemes, and to monomial torus automorphisms for $w_0,w_0^{-1}$. These restrictions preserve multiplication: both sides of each homomorphism diagram agree over $\mathbf Q$ by conjugation, and [lemma-nagata-ext-scheme-theoretically-dominant-separated] gives equality over $\mathbf Z$. Its hypotheses hold: $C$ is affine, with Laurent-polynomial coordinate ring, so separated; all relevant domains are opens of products of affine spaces and split tori over $\mathbf Z$, whose coordinate rings inject into their rationalizations. Their generic fibres are therefore scheme-theoretically dense. The same cited uniqueness applies on $f^{-1}(W')\subset W$ to $gf$ and the inclusion into $C$, and on $g^{-1}(W)\subset W'$ to $fg$ and the inclusion, proving both stated inverse identities. Since the subgroup images lie wholly in $W,W'$, these identities make the subgroup restrictions inverse group isomorphisms.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9, p.222: flat generic-fibre equality, expanded using the separated-target uniqueness lemma (Stacks Tag 01RH).

proof.text: Each coordinate inclusion sends its identity to $(0,1,0)$ by the one-sign identity in [lem-sfb-rational-chevalley-one-sign-integrality]. Every simple chart fixes this section by [lem-sfb-integral-simple-reflection-gauss-chart], and hence $f(e)=g(e)=e$. If $\Phi$ is empty, the spanning condition forces $M=0$; take $n=1$, $W=W'=C$ and $f=g=\operatorname{id}$. All equations then are identities on $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$. Every construction above uses only the given one-sign laws, torus actions and the rank-one charts; it requires no opposite-sign law on $C$.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.9, identity section and empty-root boundary case.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q102-627b4d245 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: Read the item, the new node lem-sfb-integral-simple-reflection-gauss-chart and every cited statement. No local copy of Conrad's Reductive group schemes exists, so I fetched the PDF read-only and read printed pp.219-222 (Lemmas 6.3.6, 6.3.8 with (6.3.4), and 6.3.9). Both source corrections are right. First, the product of the simple reflections is not w_0 (in type A2, s_a s_b has order 3). Second, f' must be conjugation by n^{-1}, not n. Step 1 is a correct counting argument: a maximizing w with some w^{-1}a positive gives a contradiction, then cardinality finishes it, using the finite Weyl group node. Step 2 sets up the induction explicitly, and the support clause keeps the whole of E_± in each domain. Step 3: n_a^4=1 makes h_a^3 conjugation by n_a^{-1}, applied in reverse order. Step 4 applies the Nagata uniqueness lemma's dominant-morphism form to Z-flat domains with separated affine target C. Step 5 is elementary. I checked the new node by hand in SL2 with the one-sign node's signs: n_a=[[0,1],[-1,0]], n_a^2=a^∨(-1), and the chart locus is d=1+vuχ_a(t), as in Conrad. I proved the support clause independently by a weight/closed-subset argument, and tested it on A1, the mixed-sign A2 system P=s_aΦ^+, and characteristics 2 and 3. The new node is statement-only and self-contained, with B1-B9 satisfied and no duplicate. rank-one-normalized-gauss-chart and split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus both need a reductive group over the base, so neither duplicates it, and it is strictly smaller than the item. Batch-5 flag: both flagged citations (finite-root-datum-weyl-group, pinned-split-root-realization) reach the trace-formula chapter only through lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent. That is a Mathlib leaf (Stacks 02VL, smoothness descends along fpqc covers) and part of neither assumption, so both citations are outside the assumptions. I accept the Nagata lemma as a tool_use. No SGA source is used. No changes.
